case: A 58-year-old woman comes to the physician because of recurrent sinusitis, two episodes of pneumonia over the past 18 months, and 4 months of watery diarrhea. She had no serious infections before age 55. Stool antigen testing is positive for Giardia lamblia. A chest CT obtained during her last pneumonia shows a 6-cm, well-circumscribed soft tissue mass in the anterior mediastinum behind the manubrium. Laboratory studies show IgG 210 mg/dL (700 to 1600), IgA less than 10 mg/dL (70 to 400), and IgM 18 mg/dL (40 to 230). Flow cytometry shows CD19+ B cells 3/µL (about 100 to 500) and a CD4:CD8 ratio of 0.6 (1.0 to 3.5). CT-guided biopsy of the mass shows thymoma. Diagnosis: thymoma with Good syndrome (adult-onset hypogammaglobulinemia).

questions.stem: Before the biopsy, the radiologist's differential diagnosis included the other common masses of this mediastinal compartment. Which of the following findings most strongly favors thymoma over those other masses?
options: Coexisting acquired hypogammaglobulinemia
Fat, fluid, and calcification within the mass
Continuity of the mass with a cervical goiter
Night sweats with bulky cervical lymphadenopathy
approach: Place the mass: anterior mediastinum behind the manubrium is where the adult thymus sits.
List the classic anterior mediastinal masses: thymoma, teratoma, lymphoma, and retrosternal thyroid.
Match each option to one of those masses and pick the feature that belongs to thymoma.
questions.why: The adult thymus lies in the anterior and superior mediastinum behind the manubrium, so thymoma is one of the classic masses there. Thymoma is the one most often linked to paraneoplastic immune disorders, such as myasthenia gravis, pure red cell aplasia, and hypogammaglobulinemia (Good syndrome). An anterior mediastinal mass in an older adult with new low immunoglobulins points strongly to thymoma.
whyNot: Correct.
Fat, fluid, and calcification (sometimes teeth) inside the mass are typical of a mature cystic teratoma, which also arises in the anterior mediastinum, usually in younger patients.
A mass continuous with an enlarged thyroid in the neck is a retrosternal goiter, which extends down into the superior and anterior mediastinum.
B symptoms with bulky nodes elsewhere suggest lymphoma, such as nodular sclerosis Hodgkin lymphoma, another classic anterior mediastinal mass.

questions.stem: A cervical lymph node is removed during her evaluation. Its histology is compared with that of a node from an infant with 22q11.2 deletion syndrome and severe T cell deficiency. Which of the following pairs best describes the region most depleted in each node?
options: Hers: paracortex; infant's: cortical follicles
Hers: medullary sinuses; infant's: paracortex
Hers: cortical follicles; infant's: paracortex
Hers: paracortex; infant's: medullary cords
approach: Identify the missing cell in each patient: she has almost no B cells, and the infant has almost no T cells.
Recall where each cell lives in a node: B cells in cortical follicles and germinal centers, T cells in the paracortex.
Predict depletion of the zone that belongs to the missing cell.
questions.why: Lymph node zones are organized by cell type. B cells form the cortical follicles, and germinal centers form there when B cells respond to antigen. T cells fill the paracortex between and below the follicles, around the high endothelial venules. With almost no B cells, her follicles and germinal centers are small or absent. In DiGeorge syndrome the thymus fails to develop, so few T cells reach the nodes and the paracortex is depleted.
whyNot: This reverses the two patients. A depleted paracortex fits T cell deficiency, and absent follicles fit B cell deficiency.
Medullary sinuses are lymph channels lined by macrophages and are not the main home of either B or T cells, so neither deficiency empties them.
Correct.
Her missing cell is the B cell, so her follicles are depleted. Medullary cords hold plasma cells, which come from B cells, so they would be affected in her, not in the T cell deficient infant.

topics: Lymph node zones and their cells

questions.stem: Common variable immunodeficiency was considered before the mediastinal mass was found. Which of the following findings in this patient argues most strongly against that diagnosis?
options: Onset of recurrent infections after age 50
Chronic diarrhea caused by Giardia lamblia
Low serum levels of both IgG and IgA
Very low circulating B cell count
approach: Recall the defect in CVID: B cells are present in normal or near normal numbers but fail to become plasma cells.
Check each finding against CVID: adult onset, Giardia, and low IgG and IgA all fit.
The finding that does not fit is near absence of B cells, which points to another cause such as thymoma.
questions.why: In common variable immunodeficiency, most patients have normal numbers of circulating B cells, but those cells do not differentiate into antibody-secreting plasma cells. CVID often starts in adulthood and causes low IgG and IgA, recurrent sinopulmonary infections, and Giardia diarrhea, along with higher risk of autoimmune disease and lymphoma. Good syndrome looks similar clinically, but B cells are very low or absent. Her B cell count of 3/µL is the finding that best separates the two.
whyNot: CVID often begins in adulthood, so late onset is consistent with CVID. Onset in the first year of life would point instead to X-linked agammaglobulinemia or SCID.
Giardia diarrhea is a classic CVID infection because secretory IgA is missing from the gut, so this finding supports CVID.
Low IgG and IgA are the defining laboratory features of CVID, so they fit that diagnosis.
Correct.

topics: B cell counts in antibody deficiencies

questions.stem: She begins monthly intravenous immunoglobulin prepared from pooled donor plasma. Over the next 6 months she has no further pneumonia, but her Giardia diarrhea returns after each course of antiparasitic treatment. Which of the following best explains the difference in protection?
options: IgG in the product cannot fix complement on bacteria
The product supplies no secretory IgA to the gut lumen
IgM in the product is too large to reach the lung tissue
IgE in the product is needed for defense against protozoa
approach: Recall what intravenous immunoglobulin contains: almost entirely monomeric IgG.
Ask which isotype protects each site: IgG in blood and tissues, secretory IgA on mucosal surfaces.
Giardia lives in the intestinal lumen, where infused IgG does not supply the needed secretory IgA.
questions.why: Intravenous immunoglobulin is mostly IgG, which circulates in blood and tissue fluid, opsonizes bacteria, and fixes complement. That is why her pneumonias stopped. Secretory IgA is a dimer joined by J chain, made by plasma cells in the lamina propria and carried into the lumen by the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor. Infused IgG cannot replace it, so mucosal infections such as giardiasis often continue in patients on replacement therapy.
whyNot: IgG fixes complement through the classical pathway and opsonizes bacteria. These actions are part of why her pneumonias stopped.
Correct.
Intravenous immunoglobulin contains very little IgM. Lung protection here comes from IgG, which does reach lung tissue.
Intravenous immunoglobulin contains essentially no IgE, and IgE is the defense against helminths, not intestinal protozoa such as Giardia.

topics: Antibody isotypes and their sites of action

dx: X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency (IL2RG common gamma chain mutation)
case: A 5-month-old boy is brought to the physician because of poor weight gain, persistent oral thrush, and chronic diarrhea. Newborn screening reported absent T cell receptor excision circles, but follow-up was missed. A maternal uncle died of infection in infancy. Temperature is 38.4 °C (101.1 °F), pulse is 168/min, respirations are 56/min, and oxygen saturation is 88% on room air. Chest x-ray shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates and no thymic shadow. Bronchoalveolar lavage shows Pneumocystis jirovecii. Lymphocyte count is 1,400/mm3 (normal for age about 4,000 to 13,500). Flow cytometry shows nearly absent CD3+ T cells and CD56+ NK cells, with normal numbers of CD19+ B cells. Serum IgA and IgM are undetectable. Genetic testing shows a hemizygous IL2RG mutation. Diagnosis: X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency.

questions.stem: A second infant with severe combined immunodeficiency has biallelic loss-of-function mutations in RAG1. Which of the following lymphocyte patterns is most likely in the second infant?
options: T cells absent, B cells present, NK cells absent
T cells absent, B cells absent, NK cells absent
T cells absent, B cells absent, NK cells present
T cells present, B cells absent, NK cells present
approach: Recall what RAG1 does: it cuts DNA to start V(D)J recombination of T cell and B cell receptor genes.
Both T cells and B cells need a rearranged receptor to develop, so both are absent.
NK cells do not rearrange receptor genes, so they develop normally.
questions.why: RAG1 and RAG2 make the recombinase that starts V(D)J recombination. Without it, neither T cells nor B cells can build an antigen receptor, so both are absent (T-, B-, NK+ SCID). NK cells use germline-encoded receptors and are spared. In this patient, the common gamma chain is shared by the receptors for IL-2, IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15, and IL-21. Loss of IL-7 signaling blocks T cell development and loss of IL-15 signaling blocks NK cells, while B cells still form (T-, B+, NK-). All forms of SCID have low T cell receptor excision circles.
whyNot: This is the pattern of X-linked SCID from IL2RG mutation (and of JAK3 deficiency), the pattern of this patient.
Loss of all three lymphocyte types fits adenosine deaminase deficiency, in which toxic purine metabolites kill all lymphocytes.
Correct.
T cells also need RAG to rearrange their receptor genes, so they cannot be present in RAG deficiency.

questions.stem: He develops anemia and needs a red blood cell transfusion before a stem cell transplant can be arranged. If the transfused blood is not irradiated, which of the following complications is he at greatest risk of developing?
options: Rash, diarrhea, liver injury, and marrow aplasia
Fever and back pain from intravascular hemolysis
Acute hypoxemia with bilateral pulmonary edema
Urticaria, wheezing, and hypotension within minutes
approach: Note that donor blood contains living donor T cells unless it is irradiated.
An infant with no T cells cannot reject those cells, so they engraft and attack him.
That is transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease, which targets skin, gut, liver, and marrow.
questions.why: Cellular blood products contain viable donor lymphocytes. A normal recipient destroys them, but an infant with SCID has no T cells to do so. The donor T cells engraft, recognize his HLA as foreign, and attack the skin, gut, liver, and bone marrow. Marrow involvement causes pancytopenia, and the condition is usually fatal. Irradiation stops donor lymphocytes from dividing, so infants with SCID receive only irradiated, CMV-safe products and are also never given live vaccines.
whyNot: Correct.
Acute hemolysis comes from ABO-incompatible blood and preformed antibodies. Irradiation does not prevent it, and this infant makes few antibodies.
This describes transfusion-related acute lung injury, caused by donor antibodies activating recipient neutrophils in the lungs. Irradiation does not prevent it.
This is an anaphylactic reaction, for example in IgA-deficient patients with anti-IgA antibodies. It needs antibodies made by the recipient, which he cannot produce.

questions.stem: An autopsy report on his maternal uncle describes a small thymus with epithelial cells present but very few lymphocytes, no corticomedullary distinction, and no Hassall corpuscles. Which of the following normal steps of fetal thymic development most likely failed?
options: Budding of thymic epithelium from the third pharyngeal pouch
Expansion of marrow-derived precursors within the epithelium
Investment of the gland by a neural crest capsule and septa
Descent of the paired primordia into the anterior mediastinum
approach: Separate the two parts of the thymus: an epithelial framework from endoderm and lymphocytes that come from the bone marrow.
The epithelium is present, so the endodermal framework formed.
What is missing is the lymphoid part, which needs marrow precursors to colonize the framework and expand.
questions.why: The thymic epithelium forms from third pharyngeal pouch endoderm. Bone marrow derived T cell precursors then migrate in during fetal life, multiply, and mature. Their growth fills the cortex with packed thymocytes and creates the cortex and medulla, and Hassall corpuscles form in the medulla. In X-linked SCID, precursors that lack IL-7 receptor signaling cannot survive and expand, so the epithelial framework is left almost empty. In DiGeorge syndrome, by contrast, the epithelium itself is missing.
whyNot: The report describes epithelial cells, so budding from the third pouch occurred. Failure of this step is the DiGeorge pattern, with no thymic epithelium at all.
Correct.
Neural crest forms the capsule and septa. Its loss would affect the connective tissue framework, and it would not explain the absent lymphocytes.
Failed descent gives an ectopic thymus in the neck, which can still contain normal lymphocytes.

topics: Thymus in SCID versus DiGeorge syndrome

questions.stem: His thymus lacks the normal division into cortex and medulla. In a normal infant thymus, a pale-staining region contains loosely packed mature T cells that express either CD4 or CD8 but not both. Which of the following structures is also characteristic of this region?
options: Epithelial cells forming a blood-thymus barrier
Densely packed CD4+CD8+ thymocytes
Subcapsular sinus receiving afferent lymph
Keratinized whorls of epithelial cells
approach: Identify the region: pale staining with loosely packed single-positive mature T cells is the medulla.
Recall the structures of the medulla: Hassall corpuscles, which are keratinized whorls of epithelial cells.
questions.why: The thymic cortex stains dark because it is packed with immature thymocytes, many of them CD4+CD8+ double positive. The medulla stains paler and holds fewer, more mature single-positive T cells that have passed positive selection. Hassall corpuscles, concentric whorls of keratinized epithelial cells, are found only in the medulla and are the classic marker of this region.
whyNot: The blood-thymus barrier surrounds capillaries in the cortex, where it shields developing thymocytes from blood-borne antigen.
Dense double-positive thymocytes make the cortex dark, which is the opposite of this pale region.
A subcapsular sinus receiving afferent lymph belongs to a lymph node. The thymus has no afferent lymphatics.
Correct.

dx: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1 (CD18 integrin defect)
case: A 6-week-old girl is brought to the physician because of redness and swelling around her umbilical cord stump, which has not yet separated. Her parents are first cousins. Temperature is 38.3 °C (100.9 °F), pulse is 164/min, and respirations are 40/min. The periumbilical skin is red, warm, and indurated, with no fluctuance and no pus. Leukocyte count is 48,000/mm3 (normal for age about 5,000 to 19,500) with 80% neutrophils, which look normal on the blood smear. Flow cytometry shows absent CD18 on her neutrophils and lymphocytes. A dihydrorhodamine test of neutrophil oxidative burst is normal. Diagnosis: leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1.

questions.stem: Intravital microscopy of an inflamed venule in a child with this disorder would most likely show neutrophils doing which of the following?
options: Adhering firmly but failing to cross the endothelium
Remaining in the axial stream without any contact
Crossing the wall but failing to move toward C5a
Rolling along the endothelium without firm arrest
approach: List the steps of extravasation: margination, selectin-mediated rolling, integrin-mediated firm adhesion, transmigration, chemotaxis.
CD18 is the beta2 chain of the leukocyte integrins such as LFA-1 and Mac-1.
Rolling uses selectins and still works; the first step that fails is firm adhesion.
questions.why: Neutrophils first roll along activated endothelium as selectins bind their sugar ligands. Chemokines then activate beta2 integrins (LFA-1 and Mac-1, which share CD18) so that they bind ICAM-1 strongly, which stops the cell. Without CD18, neutrophils roll but cannot arrest, so they never leave the vessel. This explains the high blood neutrophil count, the lack of pus at the infected site, and delayed separation of the cord stump.
whyNot: Firm adhesion is exactly the step that needs CD18 integrins, so these cells cannot adhere firmly in the first place.
Margination and selectin-mediated contact with the wall are intact, so neutrophils do touch and roll on the endothelium.
Her neutrophils never cross the wall. Normal crossing with poor movement toward chemoattractants would instead suggest a chemotaxis defect, as in Chediak-Higashi syndrome.
Correct.

questions.stem: Her lymphocytes also lack CD18. Naive T cells normally enter lymph nodes across high endothelial venules. Which of the following steps in that entry most directly depends on the molecule she lacks?
options: Tethering of L-selectin to peripheral node addressin
Firm arrest after CCR7 chemokine signaling
Recognition of antigen carried in by dendritic cells
Exit from the node into efferent lymphatic vessels
approach: Recall the homing steps at high endothelial venules: L-selectin tethering, chemokine activation through CCR7, integrin arrest, then crossing into the paracortex.
CD18 is part of the integrin LFA-1.
The step that needs LFA-1 is firm arrest after CCR7 signaling switches the integrin to its high-affinity state.
questions.why: Naive T cells home to lymph nodes through the high endothelial venules of the paracortex. L-selectin on the T cell tethers to addressins on the venule, and chemokines on the endothelium bind CCR7. That signal turns on LFA-1 (CD11a/CD18), which binds ICAM-1 and stops the cell so it can cross into the node. There it scans dendritic cells that carried antigen in through afferent lymph, and it later leaves through efferent lymph.
whyNot: Tethering uses L-selectin, which is not an integrin and does not contain CD18.
Correct.
Antigen recognition uses the T cell receptor and MHC on dendritic cells after the T cell is already inside the node.
Exit through efferent lymph happens after the T cell is inside the node and depends on other signals, not on LFA-1 binding to venules.

questions.stem: In vitro, her neutrophils ingest bacteria coated with IgG normally but ingest bacteria coated with complement fragments poorly. Which of the following best explains this pattern?
options: Absent receptor for iC3b on the neutrophil
Defective fusion of phagosomes with lysosomes
Absent Fc gamma receptors on the neutrophil
Lack of C3 convertase activity in her serum
approach: Identify the two opsonins: IgG binds Fc gamma receptors, and C3b and iC3b bind complement receptors.
Recall that complement receptor 3 (Mac-1) is the integrin CD11b/CD18.
Loss of CD18 removes complement receptor 3, so only complement-coated particles are poorly ingested.
questions.why: Opsonins coat microbes so phagocytes can grab them. IgG binds Fc gamma receptors, and C3b and its breakdown product iC3b bind complement receptors. Complement receptor 3, also called Mac-1, is the integrin CD11b/CD18, the main receptor for iC3b. Without CD18, neutrophils cannot bind iC3b-coated bacteria well, while ingestion through Fc gamma receptors stays normal. After ingestion, the phagosome fuses with lysosomes to kill the microbe.
whyNot: Correct.
Failed phagolysosome fusion is the Chediak-Higashi defect from LYST mutation. It would affect killing of all ingested bacteria, with giant granules on the smear.
Fc gamma receptors are intact, since her neutrophils ingest IgG-coated bacteria normally.
The test compares her neutrophils with bacteria already coated with complement, so her serum C3 convertase is not involved. CD18 deficiency does not affect complement proteins.

questions.stem: Her normal dihydrorhodamine test shows an intact respiratory burst. A boy with recurrent Serratia and Staphylococcus aureus abscesses has an abnormal dihydrorhodamine test, normal NADPH oxidase genes, and episodes of hemolysis. He has less than 5% of normal activity of a cytoplasmic enzyme expressed in both red cells and neutrophils. Deficiency of which of the following enzymes most likely explains his findings?
options: Pyruvate kinase
Glutathione peroxidase
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase
Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase
approach: An abnormal dihydrorhodamine test means a weak respiratory burst, but the oxidase genes are normal.
The oxidase needs NADPH, which phagocytes make mainly in the pentose phosphate pathway.
The first and rate-limiting enzyme of that pathway is glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase, which also explains his hemolysis.
questions.why: The respiratory burst runs in steps. NADPH oxidase uses NADPH to turn oxygen into superoxide, superoxide dismutase turns superoxide into hydrogen peroxide, and myeloperoxidase combines hydrogen peroxide with chloride to make hypochlorous acid. NADPH comes mainly from the pentose phosphate pathway, which starts with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase. Very severe G6PD deficiency starves the oxidase of NADPH and produces a picture like chronic granulomatous disease, with infections by catalase-positive organisms, and it also causes hemolysis because red cells cannot protect themselves from oxidant injury.
whyNot: Pyruvate kinase deficiency causes hemolysis from low red cell ATP, but glycolysis does not make NADPH, so the neutrophil burst is normal.
Glutathione peroxidase uses glutathione to detoxify hydrogen peroxide. Its loss would not stop the burst from making oxidants.
Correct.
This glycolytic enzyme makes NADH, not NADPH, and its loss is not a known cause of a failed respiratory burst.

dx: Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 1 (AIRE mutation) with chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis and hypoparathyroidism
case: A 13-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of 3 months of fatigue, salt craving, and dizziness on standing. He has had recurrent oral thrush and candidal nail infections since age 4. Hypoparathyroidism was diagnosed after a hypocalcemic seizure at age 8, and he takes calcium and calcitriol. Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse is 112/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 86/52 mm Hg. His skin creases and gums are hyperpigmented, and there is white plaque on the tongue. Laboratory studies show sodium 128 mEq/L (135 to 145), potassium 5.8 mEq/L (3.5 to 5.0), 8 AM cortisol 2 µg/dL (5 to 25), and ACTH 480 pg/mL (10 to 60). Antibodies to 21-hydroxylase are present. Genetic testing shows biallelic AIRE mutations. Diagnosis: autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 1.

questions.stem: A different boy with a FOXP3 mutation has had severe watery diarrhea, eczematous dermatitis, and insulin-dependent diabetes since the first months of life. Which of the following is primarily defective in that boy but intact in this patient?
options: Expression of tissue-restricted antigens in the thymus
Development of suppressive regulatory T cells
Fas-mediated deletion of repeatedly activated lymphocytes
Production of IL-17 against fungi on mucosal surfaces
approach: Name the second boy's syndrome: FOXP3 mutation with enteropathy, dermatitis, and early diabetes is IPEX.
FOXP3 is the master transcription factor of regulatory T cells, a peripheral tolerance mechanism.
This patient's AIRE defect is in central tolerance, so his regulatory T cells form.
questions.why: AIRE lets medullary thymic epithelial cells express proteins normally found only in peripheral organs such as the parathyroid and adrenal. Self-reactive thymocytes that bind these proteins are deleted. Without AIRE, they escape, which causes APS-1 with chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, and adrenal insufficiency. FOXP3 is needed for regulatory T cells to develop and suppress other T cells in the periphery. Its loss causes IPEX: immune dysregulation, polyendocrinopathy, enteropathy, X-linked.
whyNot: This is the AIRE function, the defect in this patient. FOXP3 does not control thymic display of tissue antigens.
Correct.
Fas-mediated deletion is defective in autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome, which causes lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, and autoimmune cytopenias.
Loss of IL-17 activity contributes to candidiasis in this patient's disorder, through autoantibodies. It is not the primary defect in IPEX.

questions.stem: In this patient's thymus, one step of T cell selection proceeds normally and decides whether each surviving thymocyte becomes a CD4 or a CD8 T cell. Which of the following describes that step?
options: Binding of tissue antigens on medullary epithelial cells
Rearrangement of T cell receptor beta chain genes
Recognition of foreign peptide in the lymph node paracortex
Binding of self-MHC on cortical epithelial cells
approach: Sort the two selection steps: positive selection in the cortex and negative selection in the medulla.
AIRE works in the medulla, so negative selection is the step that fails in him.
Positive selection on cortical epithelial MHC is intact, and the class of MHC bound decides CD4 or CD8.
questions.why: Thymocytes start as CD4-CD8- double-negative cells, rearrange their receptor genes, and become CD4+CD8+ double-positive cells in the cortex. Cortical epithelial cells test them: cells whose receptor binds self-MHC weakly survive (positive selection), and the rest die by neglect. Binding to class I makes a CD8 cell, and binding to class II makes a CD4 cell. Single-positive cells then move to the medulla, where AIRE-driven display of tissue antigens deletes cells that bind self too strongly. That medullary step is the one that fails in this patient.
whyNot: This is negative selection, the AIRE-dependent step that fails in this patient. It removes self-reactive cells and does not set CD4 or CD8 identity.
Beta chain rearrangement happens at the double-negative stage, before cells express both CD4 and CD8, so it does not decide between them.
Foreign antigen recognition in lymph nodes happens after T cells are mature and have already committed to CD4 or CD8.
Correct.

topics: Positive and negative selection in the thymus

questions.stem: Many patients with this disorder have neutralizing autoantibodies against cytokines that recruit neutrophils and induce antimicrobial peptides in skin and mucosal epithelium. These autoantibodies most likely contribute to his chronic candidiasis by blocking products of which of the following T cell subsets?
options: Th1 cells, which secrete interferon-gamma
Th2 cells, which secrete interleukin-5
Th17 cells, which secrete interleukin-22
Regulatory T cells, which secrete interleukin-10
approach: Identify the job described: recruiting neutrophils and inducing antimicrobial peptides in epithelium.
That is the role of IL-17 and IL-22, made by Th17 cells, which defend against extracellular bacteria and fungi such as Candida.
Blocking these cytokines leaves skin, nails, and mucosa open to Candida.
questions.why: Th17 cells, induced by IL-6, TGF-beta, and IL-23, make IL-17 and IL-22. IL-17 recruits neutrophils, and IL-22 makes epithelial cells produce antimicrobial peptides. Together they protect skin and mucosa against Candida and extracellular bacteria. Most patients with APS-1 make autoantibodies that neutralize IL-17 and IL-22, which helps explain why chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis is often the first sign of the disease.
whyNot: Th1 cells and interferon-gamma activate macrophages against intracellular microbes such as mycobacteria. They are not the main defense against mucosal Candida.
Th2 cells and IL-5 drive eosinophils and IgE against helminths.
Correct.
Regulatory T cells and IL-10 suppress immune responses. Blocking them would increase inflammation, not cause candidiasis.

topics: T helper subsets and their cytokines

questions.stem: Years later, neck exploration for an unrelated thyroid nodule finds one of his inferior parathyroid glands, small and infiltrated by lymphocytes, inside the thymus in the anterior mediastinum. Which of the following best explains this location?
options: Descent with the thymus from the third pouch
Origin from the fourth pouch with the ultimobranchial body
Migration with the thyroid along the thyroglossal duct
Formation from neural crest of the aorticopulmonary septum
approach: Recall that the inferior parathyroids and the thymus both come from third pharyngeal pouch endoderm.
The thymus descends into the anterior mediastinum and pulls the inferior parathyroids down with it.
If a parathyroid fails to separate from the thymus, it is carried into the mediastinum.
questions.why: The third pharyngeal pouch forms both the thymus and the inferior parathyroid glands. As the thymus descends into the anterior mediastinum, it drags the inferior parathyroids downward, and they usually stop at the lower poles of the thyroid. This is why the inferior glands come from a higher pouch but end up lower than the superior glands, and why an ectopic inferior gland is often found in the thymus. The thymic capsule and septa come from neural crest.
whyNot: Correct.
The fourth pouch forms the superior parathyroids and the ultimobranchial body, which gives the C cells of the thyroid. These structures stay higher in the neck.
The thyroglossal duct is the path of the thyroid from the foramen cecum of the tongue. Parathyroids do not travel along it.
Neural crest forms the aorticopulmonary septum of the heart and the thymic capsule, but not parathyroid tissue.

dx: Systemic lupus erythematosus in a patient with hereditary C2 deficiency
case: A 27-year-old woman comes to the physician because of 2 months of pain in her hands and a red facial rash that worsens after sun exposure. Temperature is 37.9 °C (100.2 °F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 118/76 mm Hg. She has an erythematous rash over the cheeks and nasal bridge that spares the nasolabial folds, painless ulcers on the hard palate, and tender swelling of several metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints without deformity. Leukocyte count is 3,200/mm3 (4,500 to 11,000). Antinuclear antibody is positive at 1:640, anti-Smith antibody is positive, and anti-dsDNA is negative. Urinalysis is normal. Total hemolytic complement (CH50) is undetectable, alternative pathway activity (AH50) is normal, C3 and C4 are within reference ranges, and C2 is undetectable. Diagnosis: SLE with hereditary homozygous C2 deficiency.

questions.stem: Hereditary deficiency of which of the following other complement components would most likely predispose her to the same disease?
options: C4
C3
C7
Mannose-binding lectin
approach: Place C2 in the cascade: it is an early classical pathway component, with C1q and C4.
Early classical components help clear immune complexes and apoptotic cells.
Deficiency of any early classical component (C1q, C4, or C2) predisposes to SLE-like disease.
questions.why: C1q, C4, and C2 act early in the classical pathway. Besides fighting infection, they coat immune complexes and apoptotic cells so phagocytes can clear them. When these components are missing, nuclear material and immune complexes linger and drive autoimmunity. The risk of SLE is highest with C1q deficiency, then C4, then C2. Her normal AH50 with undetectable CH50 shows that only the classical pathway is broken.
whyNot: Correct.

C3 deficiency mainly causes severe recurrent pyogenic infections, because C3b is the key opsonin, and it can cause immune complex glomerulonephritis. It is less tied to SLE than the early classical components.
Deficiency of C5 to C9, such as C7, blocks the membrane attack complex and causes recurrent Neisseria infections.
Mannose-binding lectin deficiency causes mostly mild extra infections in early childhood, before adaptive immunity matures.

questions.stem: Which of the following best interprets her autoantibody results?
options: The ANA titer confirms SLE because ANA is highly specific
The negative anti-dsDNA result makes SLE unlikely
The anti-Smith result is highly specific for SLE
A positive anti-histone test is needed to confirm SLE
approach: Separate sensitive tests (good for ruling out) from specific tests (good for ruling in).
ANA is sensitive, anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith are specific, and anti-histone points to drug-induced lupus.
A positive specific antibody supports the diagnosis even when another specific antibody is negative.
questions.why: SLE results from poor clearance of apoptotic cells, so nuclear antigens stay exposed and drive autoantibodies that form immune complexes. ANA is positive in nearly all patients with SLE, so a negative ANA makes SLE unlikely, but it is also found in other diseases and in some healthy people. Anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith are both highly specific. Anti-dsDNA is present in only some patients and tracks with nephritis, so a negative result does not exclude SLE. Her positive anti-Smith strongly supports the diagnosis.
whyNot: ANA is sensitive, not specific. It appears in other autoimmune diseases and in some healthy people, so it cannot confirm SLE alone.
Anti-dsDNA is specific but found in only some patients, so a negative result does not rule out SLE.
Correct.
Anti-histone antibodies are typical of drug-induced lupus, for example from hydralazine or procainamide. They are not used to confirm idiopathic SLE.

topics: Sensitivity and specificity of ANA tests

questions.stem: Two years later, a new soft holosystolic murmur is heard at the cardiac apex. She has no fever, and three sets of blood cultures are negative. Which of the following findings is most likely on echocardiography?
options: Large friable vegetations perforating a leaflet
Thickened leaflets with fused commissures and short chordae
Billowing of a redundant leaflet into the left atrium
Small warty vegetations on both leaflet surfaces
approach: Link a new murmur in SLE with sterile blood cultures to Libman-Sacks endocarditis.
Recall its appearance: small, sterile, warty vegetations on either or both sides of the valve leaflets, most often the mitral valve.
questions.why: Libman-Sacks endocarditis is a nonbacterial endocarditis of SLE. Small sterile vegetations of fibrin and inflammatory cells form on the mitral or aortic valve, and unlike other vegetations they can sit on both the upper and lower surfaces of the leaflets. They can scar the valve and cause regurgitation, and they are more common with antiphospholipid antibodies. Other SLE features include malar rash, photosensitivity, nonerosive arthritis, serositis, cytopenias, and lupus nephritis.
whyNot: Large destructive vegetations fit infective endocarditis, which would be expected with fever and positive blood cultures.
Commissural fusion with short, thick chordae is chronic rheumatic heart disease, which follows repeated episodes of rheumatic fever.
A billowing redundant leaflet is mitral valve prolapse from myxomatous degeneration. It causes a midsystolic click and late systolic murmur and is not a feature of SLE.
Correct.

questions.stem: A year later, her spleen tip is palpable 4 cm below the left costal margin and her platelet count is 96,000/mm3 (150,000 to 400,000). The marrow has normal megakaryocytes. Radiolabeled platelet studies show normal platelet survival, with about 70% of labeled platelets held in the spleen (normal about 30%). Which of the following normal splenic functions, increased by splenomegaly, best explains her low platelet count?
options: Pitting of inclusions from circulating platelets
Holding a reserve pool of the body's platelets
Removal of antibody-coated platelets in the cords
Production of new platelets in the red pulp
approach: Note the clues: normal marrow production and normal platelet survival rule out low production and increased destruction.
Most labeled platelets sit in the spleen, so the platelets are pooled there.
The normal spleen stores about a third of the platelet mass, and an enlarged spleen stores more.
questions.why: The normal spleen holds about one third of the body's platelets in an exchangeable pool. When the spleen enlarges, a much larger fraction is held there, so the blood count falls even though production and survival are normal. The spleen also removes aged red cells, pits inclusions from red cells, clears opsonized and encapsulated bacteria through marginal zone B cells and macrophages, and makes IgM.
whyNot: Pitting removes inclusions such as Howell-Jolly bodies from red cells. It does not lower the platelet count.
Correct.
Destruction of antibody-coated platelets, as in immune thrombocytopenia, shortens platelet survival. Her platelet survival is normal.
The adult spleen does not normally make platelets. Extramedullary hematopoiesis occurs only in disease, such as myelofibrosis, and would not lower the count.

dx: Hyperacute rejection of a kidney allograft from preformed anti-HLA antibodies
case: A 38-year-old woman with end-stage renal disease from IgA nephropathy receives a living-donor kidney transplant from her husband after 2 years of hemodialysis. She has had three pregnancies with him and has never received a blood transfusion or a previous transplant. Donor and recipient are ABO compatible. Within 10 minutes after the vascular clamps are released, the graft, at first pink and firm, becomes mottled, cyanotic, and flaccid, and urine flow stops. The graft is removed. Retrospective testing of her pretransplant serum shows IgG antibodies against the donor's HLA class I antigens, which had been missed because of a laboratory error. Diagnosis: hyperacute rejection from preformed anti-HLA antibodies.

questions.stem: Which of the following most likely sensitized her to the donor's HLA antigens before transplantation?
options: Cross-reacting antibodies induced by gut bacterial antigens
Immune complexes deposited by her IgA nephropathy
Contact with dialyzer membranes during hemodialysis
Exposure to paternal HLA during her pregnancies
approach: Recall the three main ways to make anti-HLA antibodies: pregnancy, blood transfusion, and a previous transplant.
She had no transfusions or transplants, but she carried three fetuses fathered by the donor.
Each fetus expressed paternal HLA, which entered her circulation and induced antibodies against her husband's HLA.
questions.why: HLA antigens are inherited from both parents, so a fetus expresses the father's HLA. Fetal cells cross into the mother's blood, especially at delivery, and can induce IgG against paternal HLA. Transfusions and earlier transplants sensitize in the same way. These preformed antibodies bind graft endothelium within minutes and cause hyperacute rejection. A crossmatch tests recipient serum against donor lymphocytes before surgery to detect them, and HLA matching lowers the chance of both sensitization and later rejection.
whyNot: Gut bacteria induce natural antibodies to ABO carbohydrate antigens, the basis of ABO incompatibility. They do not induce antibodies to HLA, and she is ABO compatible.
IgA nephropathy deposits contain IgA directed at abnormal IgA1, not at donor HLA.
Dialyzer membranes can trigger complement or allergic reactions, but they carry no HLA and do not sensitize to a donor.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings is most likely on microscopic examination of the removed kidney?
options: Neutrophils and thrombi in glomerular capillaries
Interstitial lymphocytes invading tubular epithelium
Concentric intimal fibrosis narrowing the arteries
Granulomas with multinucleated giant cells
approach: Use the timing: rejection within minutes is hyperacute rejection from preformed antibody.
Antibody binding to endothelium activates complement and platelets, so the expected picture is thrombosis and neutrophils in small vessels.
questions.why: In hyperacute rejection, preformed antibodies bind HLA or ABO antigens on graft endothelium as soon as blood flows. Complement activation damages the endothelium, and platelets and neutrophils pile up. Thrombi block glomerular capillaries and arterioles, causing fibrinoid necrosis and infarction within minutes to hours. Acute rejection takes weeks to months, chronic rejection takes months to years, and graft-versus-host disease involves the skin, liver, and gut of the host instead of the graft.
whyNot: Correct.
Interstitial lymphocytes with tubulitis are acute cellular rejection, which appears weeks to months after transplant when recipient T cells respond to donor HLA.
Concentric intimal thickening is graft arteriosclerosis of chronic rejection, which develops over months to years.
Granulomas are not a pattern of kidney transplant rejection. They suggest infection such as tuberculosis or a disease such as sarcoidosis.

questions.stem: In the indirect pathway of allorecognition, recipient antigen-presenting cells process donor HLA proteins and present donor peptides to recipient CD4 T cells on MHC class II molecules. While class II molecules are assembled in the endoplasmic reticulum, which of the following keeps them from binding peptides there, so that they later load peptides in endosomes?
options: Beta2-microglobulin
Transporter associated with antigen processing
Invariant chain
Proteasome
approach: Recall the class II route: assembly in the endoplasmic reticulum, then loading in endosomes with peptides from ingested proteins.
Something must block the groove in the endoplasmic reticulum, where cytosolic peptides are present.
The invariant chain fills the groove; in the endosome it is cut down to CLIP, which HLA-DM exchanges for a peptide.
questions.why: Class I and class II molecules sample different proteins. Class I presents cytosolic proteins cut by the proteasome and pumped into the endoplasmic reticulum by TAP. Class II presents proteins taken up by endocytosis. To keep class II from binding cytosolic peptides in the endoplasmic reticulum, the invariant chain occupies its groove and guides it to endosomes. There the invariant chain is degraded, leaving the fragment CLIP, and HLA-DM removes CLIP so an endosomal peptide can bind.
whyNot: Beta2-microglobulin is the light chain of MHC class I. Class II molecules do not contain it.
TAP moves cytosolic peptides into the endoplasmic reticulum for loading onto class I molecules.
Correct.
The proteasome cuts cytosolic proteins into peptides for class I presentation. It does not block the class II groove.

topics: MHC class I and class II antigen processing

questions.stem: Her graft loss is classified in the same hypersensitivity category as which of the following reactions?
options: Generalized urticaria minutes after a bee sting
Hemolysis after an ABO-incompatible transfusion
Arthritis and fever 10 days after antithymocyte globulin
Induration 48 hours after a tuberculin skin test
approach: Identify the effector: preformed IgG binding antigens fixed on graft endothelial cells.
Antibody against a cell or tissue antigen is type II hypersensitivity.
Find the option where antibody binds antigens on cells: antibodies to ABO antigens on transfused red cells.
questions.why: Hypersensitivity is grouped by effector. Type I uses IgE on mast cells and starts within minutes. Type II uses IgG or IgM against antigens on cells or matrix. Type III uses immune complexes that deposit in vessels, and type IV uses T cells and peaks after 2 to 3 days. Hyperacute rejection is type II, because preformed antibody binds HLA on graft endothelium. An ABO-incompatible transfusion reaction works the same way, with antibody binding red cell antigens and activating complement.
whyNot: Urticaria minutes after a sting is type I, from IgE on mast cells.
Correct.
Fever and arthritis about 10 days after a foreign protein is serum sickness, a type III immune complex reaction.
Induration at 48 hours after tuberculin is type IV delayed hypersensitivity, mediated by T cells and macrophages.

dx: Acute graft-versus-host disease after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant
case: A 52-year-old woman with acute myeloid leukemia received a peripheral blood stem cell transplant from an HLA-matched unrelated donor after myeloablative conditioning, because none of her three full siblings was HLA-identical. Twenty-four days after transplant, she develops an itchy maculopapular rash that began on her palms, soles, and ears and spread to her trunk, along with watery diarrhea of about 1.5 L/day and jaundice. Total bilirubin is 4.8 mg/dL (0.1 to 1.2). Skin biopsy shows vacuolar change of the basal layer with scattered apoptotic keratinocytes next to lymphocytes. Chimerism studies show that her circulating T cells are of donor origin. Diagnosis: acute graft-versus-host disease.

questions.stem: Donor CD8 T cells kill her keratinocytes by releasing cytotoxic granules at the immunologic synapse. Which of the following events most directly allows granzyme B to trigger apoptosis of each keratinocyte?
options: Membrane attack complex insertion by complement
Perforin pores admitting granzyme to the cytoplasm
Lysozyme digestion of the keratinocyte membrane
Superoxide release into the immunologic synapse by the T cell
approach: Granzyme B is a protease that works inside the target cell, so it has to cross the target membrane.
Perforin, released from the same granules, forms pores that let granzymes enter.
Inside, granzyme B activates caspases and the cell dies by apoptosis, which matches the isolated dead keratinocytes on biopsy.
questions.why: CD8 cytotoxic T cells and NK cells kill in two main ways. In the granule pathway, perforin inserts into the target membrane and lets granzymes into the cytoplasm, where granzyme B activates caspases. In the second pathway, Fas ligand on the killer binds Fas on the target and activates caspase-8. Both pathways cause apoptosis, so single shrunken cells die with little surrounding inflammation, as seen in her skin biopsy.
whyNot: The membrane attack complex (C5b-9) is formed by complement, not by T cells, and lyses cells by making them swell rather than by delivering granzymes.
Correct.
Lysozyme digests bacterial cell walls and has no role in T cell killing.
Superoxide is made by phagocytes in the respiratory burst. Cytotoxic T cells do not kill by releasing it.

questions.stem: Over the following year her T cell count recovers slowly, and most of her new T cells have a narrow receptor repertoire. A 6-year-old receiving the same type of transplant would be expected to rebuild a broad repertoire more quickly. Which of the following best explains the difference?
options: Faster marrow homing of stem cells in children
Greater donor T cell content of pediatric grafts
Extrathymic T cell maturation in adult marrow
Fatty involution limiting her thymic output
approach: Recall the two ways T cells return after transplant: expansion of mature donor T cells, and new T cells made in the thymus from donor stem cells.
Only new thymic output gives a broad, fresh repertoire.
The adult thymus has largely involuted and been replaced by fat, so an adult depends on expansion of a few existing clones.
questions.why: The thymus is largest relative to body size in early childhood and then involutes, with its lymphoid tissue gradually replaced by adipose tissue. After puberty its output of new naive T cells falls. Established T cells survive and divide in the periphery, so immunity persists after involution or adult thymectomy. After stem cell transplant, though, a new repertoire has to be built. A child's active thymus makes many new T cells from donor precursors, while an adult relies mostly on expansion of mature donor T cells, which gives slower recovery and fewer receptor types.
whyNot: Stem cell homing and engraftment are not the reason for the T cell difference. Her marrow engrafted, and T cell recovery depends on the thymus.
Grafts are not richer in T cells for children. Expansion of mature donor T cells gives a narrow repertoire, which is her problem.
Adult marrow does not mature T cells. Conventional T cell selection requires the thymus.
Correct.

questions.stem: Despite continuous exposure to her tissue antigens, the expanded donor T cell clones do not grow without limit. When the same T cells are stimulated repeatedly, which of the following most directly removes them by apoptosis?
options: Fas ligand binding Fas on activated T cells
CTLA-4 on the T cells binding B7 on antigen-presenting cells
Interleukin-10 secreted by regulatory T cells
AIRE-driven antigen display in the thymic medulla
approach: Look for an option that kills mature, activated T cells in the periphery.
Repeated activation makes T cells express both Fas and Fas ligand, which triggers activation-induced cell death.
The other options inhibit T cells or act during thymic development.
questions.why: Repeatedly stimulated T cells express Fas (CD95) and Fas ligand. Fas ligand on one cell binds Fas on the same or a neighboring cell and activates caspase-8, causing apoptosis. This activation-induced cell death limits clonal expansion and removes self-reactive lymphocytes in the periphery. Loss-of-function FAS mutations cause autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome, with lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, autoimmune cytopenias, and increased double-negative T cells.
whyNot: Correct.
CTLA-4 binding B7 delivers an inhibitory signal and can cause anergy, but it does not directly trigger apoptosis.
IL-10 from regulatory T cells suppresses activation and cytokine production but does not delete T cells by apoptosis.
AIRE works in the thymus on developing thymocytes. It does not remove mature donor T cells in her tissues.

questions.stem: Assume that each of her three full siblings inherited HLA haplotypes independently and that no recombination occurred within the HLA region. Which of the following was the probability that at least one of them would be a full HLA match for her?
approach: Each sibling has a 1 in 4 chance of a full match, since each parent passes one of two haplotypes.
The chance that a sibling does not match is 3/4, and the chance that all three do not match is (3/4) x (3/4) x (3/4) = 27/64, about 42%.
The chance that at least one matches is 1 minus 27/64 = 37/64, about 58%.
questions.why: The HLA genes lie close together on chromosome 6 and are inherited as a block called a haplotype, one from each parent. Both haplotypes are expressed (codominant expression). A full sibling has a 25% chance of inheriting the same two haplotypes, a 50% chance of sharing one, and a 25% chance of sharing none. For several siblings, find the chance that none match and subtract it from 1. Even a fully matched sibling can cause graft-versus-host disease, because minor histocompatibility antigens outside the HLA region still differ.
whyNot: 25% is the chance that one sibling matches, not the chance that at least one of three matches.
About 42% (27/64) is the chance that none of the three siblings matches.
Correct.
75% is the chance that one sibling does not match. Adding 25% three times would also give 75%, which is the wrong way to combine probabilities.

dx: Anaphylaxis after a yellow jacket sting
case: A 34-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 15 minutes after a yellow jacket stung him on the neck while he was doing yard work. Within minutes he developed generalized hives, lip swelling, throat tightness, wheezing, and lightheadedness. A sting last summer caused only a large area of local swelling. Temperature is 37.1 °C (98.8 °F), pulse is 128/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 72/40 mm Hg. Examination shows diffuse urticaria, angioedema of the lips and eyelids, and bilateral expiratory wheezes. Serum tryptase drawn 1 hour after the sting is 38 ng/mL (less than 11.4). Later testing shows IgE against yellow jacket venom. Diagnosis: anaphylaxis after a yellow jacket sting.

questions.stem: Which of the following events at the surface of his mast cells most directly triggered their degranulation?
options: Venom antigen binding a single IgE on its receptor
C5a from venom-activated complement binding its receptor
Venom antigen cross-linking adjacent receptor-bound IgE
Venom-IgG complexes binding Fc gamma receptors
approach: Recall sensitization: after his first sting, Th2 cells and IL-4 drove B cells to make venom-specific IgE, which bound FcepsilonRI on mast cells.
On re-exposure, a multivalent antigen must bridge two or more IgE molecules to aggregate the receptors.
Receptor cross-linking starts the signal for degranulation.
questions.why: Type I hypersensitivity has two phases. During sensitization, Th2 cells make IL-4 and IL-13, B cells switch to IgE, and IgE binds the high-affinity receptor FcepsilonRI on mast cells and basophils. On re-exposure, the allergen binds and bridges neighboring IgE molecules. This cross-linking aggregates the receptors and triggers release of preformed histamine and tryptase within minutes. A late phase follows hours later, driven by newly made leukotrienes and recruited eosinophils.
whyNot: One antigen bound to a single IgE does not aggregate receptors, so it does not trigger degranulation. Cross-linking of at least two receptors is required.
C5a can degranulate mast cells directly, but his reaction depends on venom-specific IgE from prior sensitization, and venom does not work mainly through complement.
Correct.
Mast cells in human anaphylaxis are triggered mainly by IgE, not by IgG complexes. IgG-venom complexes can actually block allergen, which is part of how venom immunotherapy helps.

questions.stem: In a different patient who collapses shortly after an insect sting, which of the following combinations of findings would best distinguish anaphylaxis from a vasovagal reaction?
options: Bradycardia, pallor, and a normal serum tryptase
Tachycardia, wheezing, and a high serum tryptase
Tachycardia, perioral tingling, and carpopedal spasm
Tachycardia, fever, and a high procalcitonin level
approach: Recall what anaphylaxis looks like: urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, and hypotension with a compensatory fast pulse.
Mast cell degranulation releases tryptase, so serum tryptase rises quickly and peaks about 1 to 2 hours after the event.
A vasovagal reaction gives a slow pulse, pallor, and no mast cell activation.
questions.why: Anaphylaxis is a systemic type I reaction. Common triggers are foods such as peanut, insect stings, penicillin, and latex. Histamine and other mediators cause urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, and vasodilation with leaky vessels, so blood pressure falls and the pulse speeds up. Tryptase is stored almost only in mast cell granules, so a high serum level within a few hours of the event confirms mast cell degranulation. A vasovagal reaction is driven by vagal tone, which slows the heart and causes pallor, and tryptase stays normal.
whyNot: Bradycardia, pallor, and a normal tryptase describe a vasovagal reaction.
Correct.
Perioral tingling and carpopedal spasm suggest hyperventilation with respiratory alkalosis, which lowers ionized calcium. They do not indicate mast cell activation.
Fever with a high procalcitonin suggests bacterial sepsis, which develops over hours to days, not minutes after a sting.

questions.stem: With repeated exposure to venom proteins, the antibodies he makes against them bind with progressively higher affinity. Which of the following processes in germinal centers accounts for this increase?
options: Class switch recombination of heavy chain constant genes
V(D)J recombination in developing bone marrow B cells
Alternative splicing of heavy chain messenger RNA
Somatic hypermutation with selection for binding
approach: Venom proteins are T dependent antigens, so they produce germinal centers with T follicular helper cells.
In germinal centers, B cells mutate their variable region genes.
B cells whose mutated receptors bind antigen best get T cell help and survive, which raises affinity over time.
questions.why: In a T dependent response, helper T cells activate B cells through CD40 ligand binding CD40 and through cytokines. Activated B cells form germinal centers in lymphoid follicles. There, the enzyme activation-induced deaminase introduces point mutations into the variable region genes (somatic hypermutation). B cells with higher-affinity receptors capture more antigen, get more T cell help, and survive, which is affinity maturation. Polysaccharide antigens are T independent, produce mostly IgM, and show little affinity maturation or memory.
whyNot: Class switching changes the constant region and therefore the isotype (for example to IgE). It does not change the antigen-binding site or its affinity.
V(D)J recombination creates the first receptor in the bone marrow before the B cell ever meets antigen. It does not raise affinity after exposure.
Alternative splicing lets naive B cells express both IgM and IgD, and it switches antibody from membrane-bound to secreted form. It does not change affinity.
Correct.

questions.stem: His IgE binds yellow jacket venom antigen 5 but not honeybee venom phospholipase A2, although all of his IgE molecules bind the same receptor on mast cells. Which part of the IgE molecule accounts for this difference in antigen recognition?
options: Hypervariable regions of the variable domains
Constant domains of the epsilon heavy chains
Disulfide bonds linking the two heavy chains
Carbohydrate chains attached to the Fc portion of the molecule
approach: Separate the two jobs of an antibody: binding antigen (Fab) and binding receptors or complement (Fc).
Receptor binding is the same for all his IgE, so it is set by the shared constant region.
Antigen specificity comes from the hypervariable regions of the heavy and light chain variable domains.
questions.why: Each antibody has two identical heavy chains and two identical light chains. The Fab region holds the variable domains of both chains, and within them three hypervariable loops (complementarity-determining regions) form the antigen-binding site. These loops differ from one B cell clone to another, which is why different IgE molecules recognize different venoms. The Fc region is made of heavy chain constant domains, which set the isotype and its functions, such as IgE binding FcepsilonRI on mast cells.
whyNot: Correct.
The epsilon constant domains are the same in all his IgE and bind FcepsilonRI. They do not determine which antigen is recognized.
Disulfide bonds hold the chains together and are the same in every IgE molecule, so they cannot explain different specificities.
Fc carbohydrates affect receptor binding and stability and are not part of the antigen-binding site.

case: A 45-year-old woman comes to the physician 9 days after she received equine-derived antivenom for a venomous snakebite on her hand. She had never received animal serum products before. For 2 days she has had fever, an itchy rash, and pain in her knees, wrists, and ankles. Temperature is 38.6 °C (101.5 °F), pulse is 96/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. Examination shows an urticarial rash on the trunk and limbs, tenderness of several joints without effusion, and tender cervical and axillary lymph nodes. Laboratory studies show C3 52 mg/dL (90 to 180) and C4 6 mg/dL (16 to 47). Urinalysis shows 2+ protein with no red cell casts. Diagnosis: serum sickness after equine-derived antivenom.

questions.stem: If, instead, a small dose of horse serum had been injected into the skin of a person who already had high levels of IgG against horse proteins, which of the following would most likely develop at the site?
options: Hemorrhagic necrosis peaking at 4 to 8 hours
A wheal and flare within 15 minutes
Induration peaking at 48 to 72 hours
Tense bullae at the dermal-epidermal junction
approach: Note the setup: antigen injected locally into someone with high levels of circulating IgG.
Antigen and antibody meet in the vessel walls at the site and form immune complexes there.
That is the Arthus reaction, a local type III reaction that peaks within hours.
questions.why: Serum sickness is the systemic type III reaction. About 1 to 2 weeks after a large dose of foreign protein, new antibodies form complexes with antigen still in the blood. The complexes deposit in vessels, joints, and glomeruli, activate complement, and cause fever, urticaria, arthralgia, lymphadenopathy, proteinuria, and low complement. The Arthus reaction is the local version. When antigen enters the skin of a person who already has high IgG levels, complexes form in small vessel walls at the site, fix complement, and attract neutrophils. The result is edema, hemorrhage, and necrosis peaking at about 4 to 8 hours.
whyNot: Correct.
A wheal and flare within minutes is a type I reaction that needs IgE on mast cells. The question describes high IgG.
Induration at 48 to 72 hours is type IV delayed hypersensitivity, mediated by T cells, as in a tuberculin test.
Tense subepidermal bullae with IgG along the basement membrane is bullous pemphigoid, a type II reaction against a fixed tissue antigen.

topics: Serum sickness and the Arthus reaction

questions.stem: Which of the following initiating events best explains her low C3 and low C4 levels?
options: C3b binding factor B on bacterial cell surfaces
Spontaneous hydrolysis of C3 in plasma
Loss of C1 esterase inhibitor function
C1q binding IgG in antigen-antibody complexes
approach: Use the complement pattern: low C4 means the classical (or lectin) pathway is being used, and low C3 means the cascade is running through to C3.
Immune complexes of IgG and horse protein bind C1q, which starts the classical pathway.
Classical activation consumes C4 and C2 to make C3 convertase, which then consumes C3.
questions.why: All three complement pathways meet at C3 convertase. The classical pathway starts when C1q binds the Fc regions of IgM or IgG in immune complexes, and it uses C4 and C2 to build C4b2a. The lectin pathway starts when mannose-binding lectin binds microbial sugars and also uses C4 and C2. The alternative pathway starts with spontaneous C3 hydrolysis on microbial surfaces and uses factor B, not C4. In serum sickness, immune complexes activate the classical pathway, so both C4 and C3 fall.
whyNot: Factor B binding C3b is the alternative pathway. It consumes C3 but not C4, the pattern seen in poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.
Spontaneous C3 hydrolysis starts the alternative pathway, which does not use C4.
Loss of C1 esterase inhibitor (hereditary angioedema) lowers C4 with a normal C3 and causes swelling without fever, rash, or arthritis.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why her symptoms began about 9 days after the infusion instead of within hours?
options: Delayed recruitment of sensitized T cells to tissues
Time to mount a primary antibody response
Slow release of antivenom from the injection site
Gradual depletion of complement by the venom
approach: She had never been exposed to horse proteins, so she had no antibodies against them at the time of the infusion.
A primary response has a lag phase of about a week before antibody appears, first IgM, then IgG.
Symptoms start when new antibody meets the horse protein still circulating and forms immune complexes.
questions.why: The antivenom gave her passive immunity: ready-made horse antibodies that neutralized the venom right away. To her immune system, though, those horse antibodies were foreign proteins. In a primary response there is a lag phase of several days, then IgM appears, followed by IgG. Because the horse proteins were still in her blood when her antibodies rose, immune complexes formed and caused serum sickness at about 1 to 2 weeks. A second exposure would give a faster, larger IgG response, with higher affinity, from memory cells.
whyNot: Recruitment of sensitized T cells is the type IV mechanism. Serum sickness is caused by antibody and immune complexes, and her low complement fits that.
Correct.
Antivenom is given intravenously, so it enters the blood at once. Its slow release does not explain the delay.
Her low complement is caused by immune complexes using up complement, which happened days after the venom was neutralized.

questions.stem: Two years later she develops an itchy, red, vesicular eruption 2 days after starting topical neomycin ointment on a leg abrasion. The rash is confined to the area where the ointment was applied. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of this reaction?
options: IgE on mast cells cross-linked by the drug
IgG binding drug attached to cell surfaces
T cells reacting to drug-modified skin proteins
Drug-antibody complexes deposited in dermal vessels
approach: Use timing and location: a reaction 2 days later, only where the drug touched the skin.
Small drugs such as neomycin bind skin proteins and act as haptens.
Sensitized T cells respond to the modified proteins, which is type IV allergic contact dermatitis.
questions.why: Drug reactions can follow any of the four hypersensitivity types. Penicillin anaphylaxis is type I. Penicillin or methyldopa hemolytic anemia is type II, from IgG binding red cells. Serum sickness from foreign proteins such as chimeric monoclonal antibodies or antivenom is type III. Allergic contact dermatitis from topical neomycin is type IV: the drug binds skin proteins as a hapten, and sensitized T cells respond with cytokines that recruit macrophages. This produces a vesicular rash limited to the contact site 1 to 3 days after exposure.
whyNot: IgE cross-linking is type I and causes hives or anaphylaxis within minutes, not a vesicular rash after 2 days.
IgG binding drug on cells is type II, as in drug-induced hemolytic anemia. It does not cause a localized vesicular rash.
Correct.
Immune complex deposition is type III, like her earlier serum sickness, which gave fever, arthralgia, and low complement. It does not stay confined to a contact site.

case: A 56-year-old woman comes to the physician because of 8 years of episodes in which her fingers turn white, then blue, then red in the cold, and 2 years of heartburn and tight skin on her fingers. Temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse is 76/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg. Examination shows thickened, tight skin of the fingers and hands, a healing ulcer on the tip of the right index finger, firm white nodules in the skin of several fingers, and many telangiectasias on the face and palms. Skin of the upper arms and trunk is normal. Antinuclear antibody shows a centromere pattern, anticentromere antibodies are positive, and anti-Scl-70 antibodies are negative. Serum creatinine is 0.8 mg/dL (0.6 to 1.1). Diagnosis: limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (CREST syndrome).

questions.stem: A biopsy of the skin of her finger shows dense, compact dermal collagen with loss of adnexal structures. Which of the following mediators most directly stimulates fibroblasts to make this collagen?
options: Interferon-gamma
Interleukin-2
Granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor
Transforming growth factor-beta
approach: Recall the sequence in systemic sclerosis: endothelial injury and autoimmunity first, then fibrosis.
Activated immune cells and injured vessels release growth factors that turn fibroblasts on.
The central profibrotic signal is TGF-beta, which increases collagen and matrix production.
questions.why: Systemic sclerosis starts with small vessel endothelial injury and autoimmune activation. CD4 T cells and macrophages release cytokines, mainly TGF-beta, which activates fibroblasts and turns them into myofibroblasts that make large amounts of collagen and matrix. Fibrosis thickens the skin, scars the muscle of the esophagus (causing dysmotility and reflux), and can scar the lungs (interstitial lung disease). Narrowed small arteries explain Raynaud phenomenon and fingertip ulcers.
whyNot: Interferon-gamma activates macrophages and actually tends to reduce collagen synthesis by fibroblasts.
IL-2 drives T cell proliferation. It does not directly cause collagen production.
GM-CSF stimulates production and activation of granulocytes and macrophages, and it is not the main fibrogenic signal.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following complications is she at greatest long-term risk of developing?
options: Pulmonary arterial hypertension
Scleroderma renal crisis
Rapidly progressive skin thickening of the trunk
Erosive arthritis of the small joints of the hands
approach: Classify her disease: skin thickening limited to the hands, long-standing Raynaud, calcinosis, telangiectasia, and anticentromere antibodies mean limited (CREST) disease.
Recall the course of each type: diffuse disease brings early organ involvement and renal crisis, while limited disease progresses slowly.
The main late, life-threatening complication of limited disease is pulmonary arterial hypertension.
questions.why: Limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (CREST: calcinosis, Raynaud phenomenon, esophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, telangiectasia) has skin thickening of the hands, forearms, and face, and is linked to anticentromere antibodies. It progresses slowly, and its main serious late complication is pulmonary arterial hypertension from vascular disease of the small pulmonary arteries. Diffuse disease involves the trunk and proximal limbs, is linked to anti-Scl-70 (topoisomerase I) antibodies, and brings early interstitial lung disease and scleroderma renal crisis.
whyNot: Correct.
Scleroderma renal crisis is a feature of diffuse disease, especially early in the course with rapid skin thickening.
Skin involvement of the trunk defines diffuse disease. Limited disease stays distal to the elbows and knees, plus the face.
Joint pain can occur in systemic sclerosis, but erosive small-joint arthritis is typical of rheumatoid arthritis.

questions.stem: Her 49-year-old sister has Raynaud phenomenon, diffusely swollen hands, symmetric arthritis, and proximal muscle weakness with serum creatine kinase of 1,800 U/L (about 30 to 170). Antinuclear antibody shows a speckled pattern at 1:5,120, and anti-U1 ribonucleoprotein antibody is present at very high titer. Anti-Smith, anti-dsDNA, anticentromere, and anti-Scl-70 antibodies are negative. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in the sister?
options: Limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis
Systemic lupus erythematosus
Mixed connective tissue disease
Polymyositis
approach: Group the findings: Raynaud and swollen hands (like systemic sclerosis), arthritis (like SLE), and myositis (like polymyositis).
Overlapping features of three diseases with high-titer anti-U1 RNP define mixed connective tissue disease.
The negative disease-specific antibodies argue against each single disease.
questions.why: Mixed connective tissue disease combines features of SLE, systemic sclerosis, and polymyositis. Typical findings are Raynaud phenomenon, puffy swollen hands, arthritis, and inflammatory myositis. The marker is a very high titer of anti-U1 RNP antibodies, often with a speckled ANA, while antibodies specific to the single diseases, such as anti-Smith, anti-dsDNA, anticentromere, and anti-Scl-70, are absent.
whyNot: Limited systemic sclerosis would show sclerodactyly and usually anticentromere antibodies, which she lacks, and it does not explain her marked myositis.
SLE would usually show anti-dsDNA or anti-Smith antibodies, which are negative, and SLE alone does not explain prominent myositis with swollen hands.
Correct.
Polymyositis explains her weakness and high creatine kinase, but not the combination of Raynaud phenomenon, swollen hands, and arthritis with very high anti-U1 RNP.

questions.stem: Her risk of making anticentromere antibodies is linked to inheritance of certain HLA class II alleles. Which of the following best explains how an HLA class II allele can increase the risk of autoimmunity?
options: It encodes the self protein that becomes the autoantigen
Its groove presents a self peptide well to CD4 T cells
It prevents assembly of class I molecules with beta2-microglobulin
It lowers the threshold for complement activation
approach: Recall what an HLA class II molecule does: it binds peptides in its groove and shows them to CD4 T cells.
Different alleles have different groove shapes, so each binds a different set of peptides.
An allele that binds and displays a particular self peptide well makes it easier to activate self-reactive helper T cells when tolerance fails.
questions.why: Autoimmunity develops when central or peripheral tolerance fails, and genes and environment both add risk. HLA genes are the strongest genetic factor for many autoimmune diseases. Each class II allele has a groove that binds a particular range of peptides. An allele that presents a self peptide efficiently can help self-reactive CD4 T cells become activated, and those cells then help B cells make high-affinity IgG autoantibodies. Infections can add to this through molecular mimicry, as with group A streptococcal M protein in rheumatic fever.
whyNot: HLA genes encode the presenting molecules, not the autoantigens. Centromere proteins are encoded by other genes.
Correct.
Class II alleles do not affect assembly of class I molecules, which pair with beta2-microglobulin in the endoplasmic reticulum.
HLA molecules are not complement regulators. Complement regulation does not explain how an HLA allele raises autoimmune risk.
